title: UNIT 6: TRANSFORMATIONS OF THE PLANE
notes:
✓ Transformation → a rule that moves every point of a plane figure to a new position.

◆ Original point → pre-image.
◆ New point → image.
◆ Transformation → maps points of the plane to other points.

Main transformations studied:
1. Translation
2. Reflection
3. Rotation

These transformations are used to move points, lines, circles and other plane figures while studying how their positions and properties change.

title: 6.1 BASIC CONCEPTS OF TRANSFORMATIONS
notes:
✓ A transformation changes the position of points in the plane according to a definite rule.

◆ Pre-image → the original figure.
◆ Image → the transformed figure.
◆ Transformation T → maps a point P to its image P′.

Written as:
T(P) = P′

Example:
If T moves A(2,3) to A′(5,6), then the transformation has mapped A to A′.

A transformation can be applied to an individual point or to every point of a geometric figure.

title: RIGID TRANSFORMATIONS
notes:
✓ Rigid transformation → a transformation that preserves distances and therefore preserves the size and shape of a figure.

The main rigid transformations are:

◆ Translation → slides a figure.
◆ Reflection → flips a figure.
◆ Rotation → turns a figure.

Under a rigid transformation:
◆ lengths remain unchanged
◆ angles remain unchanged
◆ shape remains unchanged
◆ size remains unchanged

→ A transformed figure is congruent to its original figure.

title: 6.2 TRANSLATION
notes:
✓ Translation → moves every point of a figure the same distance in the same direction.

A translation is represented by a vector:
T = (a,b)

The point:
P(x,y)
becomes:
P′(x+a, y+b).

Example:
Translate P(2,3) by T=(4,−1).

P′ = (2+4, 3−1)
   = (6,2).

→ Translation changes position but preserves size, shape and orientation.

title: TRANSLATING PLANE FIGURES
notes:
To translate a figure:

1. Identify the translation vector.
2. Add its horizontal component to every x-coordinate.
3. Add its vertical component to every y-coordinate.
4. Connect the transformed points in the same order.

Example:
A(1,2), B(4,2), C(2,5)

Translation T=(3,−2):

A′=(4,0)
B′=(7,0)
C′=(5,3)

→ Every point moves by exactly the same vector.

title: 6.3 REFLECTION
notes:
✓ Reflection → flips a figure across a line called the line of reflection.

The line of reflection acts like a mirror.
Each point and its image are the same distance from the line.
The segment joining a point to its image is perpendicular to the line of reflection.

Reflection preserves:
◆ lengths
◆ angles
◆ size
◆ shape

→ Orientation is reversed.

title: STANDARD REFLECTION RULES
notes:
For a point P(x,y):

◆ Reflection in x-axis:
(x,y) → (x,−y)

◆ Reflection in y-axis:
(x,y) → (−x,y)

◆ Reflection in y=x:
(x,y) → (y,x)

◆ Reflection in y=−x:
(x,y) → (−y,−x)

Example:
P(3,−2) reflected in the x-axis:
P′=(3,2).

✓ Memorize these four standard reflection rules.

title: REFLECTION IN A GENERAL LINE
notes:
✓ A reflection can also be made in a line other than the coordinate axes.

For reflection in a line such as y=mx, the image is determined using the perpendicular relationship between a point and the mirror line.

Important idea:
The line of reflection is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a point and its image.

Therefore:
◆ P and P′ are equally distant from the mirror line.
◆ PP′ ⟂ line of reflection.

→ Always identify the reflection line before finding the image.

title: 6.4 ROTATION
notes:
✓ Rotation → turns every point of a figure through the same angle about a fixed point called the centre of rotation.

◆ Centre → fixed point.
◆ Angle of rotation → amount of turning.
◆ Direction → clockwise or counterclockwise.

Rotation preserves:
◆ distance from the centre
◆ lengths
◆ angles
◆ size and shape.

Example:
A point rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin moves according to the 90° rotation rule.

title: ROTATIONS ABOUT THE ORIGIN
notes:
For P(x,y), counterclockwise rotations about the origin follow these rules:

◆ 90°:
(x,y) → (−y,x)

◆ 180°:
(x,y) → (−x,−y)

◆ 270°:
(x,y) → (y,−x)

◆ 360°:
(x,y) → (x,y)

Example:
P(2,3) rotated 90° counterclockwise:
P′=(−3,2).

→ Clockwise rotation can be treated as a counterclockwise rotation through 360°−θ.

title: ROTATION ABOUT ANY CENTRE
notes:
To rotate a point about a centre other than the origin:

1. Translate the centre to the origin.
2. Apply the required rotation.
3. Translate the point back.

General idea:
Centre C(h,k), point P(x,y).

First work with the displacement from C to P:
(x−h, y−k).

Apply the rotation rule to this displacement, then add (h,k) back.

→ This method works for rotations about any point in the plane.

title: COMBINING TRANSFORMATIONS
notes:
✓ More than one transformation can be applied successively to the same figure.

Example:
A point may be:
1. translated
2. then reflected
3. then rotated.

✓ The order matters.

For example:
Reflection followed by rotation generally gives a different result from rotation followed by reflection.

→ When solving a composite transformation, apply the first transformation completely, then use the resulting image as the input for the next transformation.

title: EFFECTS ON COORDINATES
notes:
✓ Transformation rules can be applied directly to coordinates.

◆ Translation T=(a,b):
(x,y) → (x+a,y+b)

◆ Reflection in x-axis:
(x,y) → (x,−y)

◆ Reflection in y-axis:
(x,y) → (−x,y)

◆ Reflection in y=x:
(x,y) → (y,x)

◆ 90° counterclockwise rotation:
(x,y) → (−y,x)

◆ 180° rotation:
(x,y) → (−x,−y)

→ Coordinate rules make transformations faster to calculate.

title: TRANSFORMING LINES AND CIRCLES
notes:
✓ Transformations can be applied to complete geometric figures, not only individual points.

◆ Lines → transform their points to obtain the image line.
◆ Circles → transform the centre and radius appropriately.
◆ Plane figures → transform all important vertices or points.

Rigid transformations preserve the radius of a circle.

Example:
A circle with centre (2,3) and radius 4 translated by (5,−1) has:
New centre = (7,2)
New radius = 4.

→ Translation changes position but not size.

title: IDENTIFYING A TRANSFORMATION
notes:
✓ You can identify a transformation by observing how the figure changes.

◆ Same direction and same distance for every point → Translation.

◆ Figure is flipped across a line → Reflection.

◆ Figure turns around a fixed centre → Rotation.

◆ If distances are preserved, the transformation is rigid.

Exam tip:
Look for the fixed point, mirror line, or common displacement before calculating coordinates.

title: SYMMETRY AND TRANSFORMATIONS
notes:
✓ Symmetry → a property in which a figure remains unchanged under a particular transformation.

◆ Line symmetry → reflection produces the same figure.

◆ Rotational symmetry → rotation through a certain angle produces the same figure.

Example:
A square has:
• reflection symmetry
• rotational symmetry.

→ Transformations provide a mathematical way to describe symmetry and repeating patterns.

title: WORKED EXAMPLE: COMBINED MOVEMENT
notes:
Given P(2,1):

Step 1. Translate by T=(3,2):
P′=(5,3).

Step 2. Reflect P′ in the x-axis:
P″=(5,−3).

✓ Final image:
P″=(5,−3).

→ Always apply composite transformations in the order given.

Do not combine the rules before checking which transformation is applied first.

title: UNIT 6 KEY FORMULAS & QUICK REVISION
notes:
◆ Transformation → maps each point to an image point.

◆ Rigid transformation → preserves distance, size and shape.

◆ Translation:
(x,y) → (x+a,y+b)

◆ Reflection in x-axis:
(x,y) → (x,−y)

◆ Reflection in y-axis:
(x,y) → (−x,y)

◆ Reflection in y=x:
(x,y) → (y,x)

◆ Reflection in y=−x:
(x,y) → (−y,−x)

◆ 90° counterclockwise:
(x,y) → (−y,x)

◆ 180°:
(x,y) → (−x,−y)

◆ 270°:
(x,y) → (y,−x)

◆ 360°:
(x,y) → (x,y)

◆ Translation → slide.
◆ Reflection → flip.

◆ Composite transformation → apply transformations in the stated order.
